doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Lack of practice time and the value of classical study
summary: Hanna says he has not had time to practice for ten years, describes his classical routine, and advises a student to study Chopin and Rachmaninoff.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yeah, we were just talking about tributes. Be careful who you pay tribute to. You just were saying some very well thought out phrases about different piano players and I have to say it sounded to me like you were describing yourself.

Oh no, no, no, not me yet. You know I’ll tell you, I’ve worked hard at the piano. I’ve been working almost all my life trying to play the piano. And just when you think you’re getting there, you’re getting to a place where you can do whatever you want to do, something happens that usually you have no control over. And for the last ten, twelve years, I haven’t been able to practice. I’m going to start back. But I haven’t been able to practice. I’ve been working hard and teaching a lot, and there’s no time for me to sit, as I used to. I used to, like for instance, if I were going to go and play a gig, say California or Japan, I used to sit and practice Chopin etudes and play Bach and just run through my Mozart or play a Beethoven sonata, maybe two or three times, and get my chops up, get my head up. And the reason I practice the classical music is because there are so many nuances and differences and changes to go through. Different minds coming together with music, and whenever I would play I had control over the piano, rather than the piano having control over me. But now I don’t get a chance to practice. Boy it’s like you’ve got five thousand pounds on your back. I mean I still want to do the same ideas, but they don’t all come out. That’s why I was talking about those guys — Monty Alexander and — what’s his name — Petrucciani, and there’s another one too, a young fellow who was a student of mine — oh boy names start to slip away — but he’s a wonderful player. I

explained to him years ago, I can’t even think of how long ago it was but it was more than twenty years ago, I said if you really want to get a control and command, play some Scriabin, play some Faure, play some Rachmaninoff, play some Chopin. Spend time practicing Chopin. They knew what the piano was about. And I told him just like that and he took me to heart. The next thing I know he had a beautiful album out, Faure, Chopin, Rachmaninoff. Yeah it was great, too, to hear that. He took the chords and form and shape of the pieces and he paid tribute to these guys. I thought it was wonderful.
